target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Automated a production EventBridge fine-tuning loop for a Bedrock document-importance classifier, retraining only when a larger LLM’s cross-model eval scores move past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: Two noun stacks in one sentence: 'production EventBridge fine-tuning loop' and 'Bedrock document-importance classifier'. 'a larger LLM’s cross-model eval scores move past a threshold' hides the mechanism: it is not said what the larger LLM scores, what it is compared against, or which way the threshold is crossed.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Nobody says this sentence out loud. A reader has to unpack it backwards to learn that a model ranks documents by importance and is retrained automatically. The trigger condition is the interesting design choice, and it is the part a reader can't follow, so an interviewer's first question will be 'what does that actually mean?'
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the larger LLM evaluates (the classifier's labels? a held-out set?) and what 'cross-model' compares
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say what the classifier does in plain words first, then how retraining is triggered, then name the services. Example shape: 'Set up automatic retraining for the model that ranks which documents matter most, triggered on EventBridge only when a larger LLM's grading of its output drops below a threshold'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built a Python pipeline for PhysTwin (PhD-led digital twin, targeting ICLR) turning AnyGrasp output on multi-camera images into Open3D overlays for a VLM; tuned its prompts to pick correct grasps and judge depth
bullet_feedback.problem: The parenthetical '(PhD-led digital twin, targeting ICLR)' puts context mid-sentence, and the chain 'AnyGrasp output on multi-camera images into Open3D overlays for a VLM' is four proper nouns in a row. The semicolon tacks on a second task. 'its prompts' is ambiguous: it could refer to the pipeline or to the VLM.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A non-ML recruiter can't restate this bullet. An engineer has to parse it twice to see that the candidate draws candidate robot grasps onto 3D views so a vision-language model can choose one. There is also no outcome, so the bullet ends on a task.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the system is for (robot grasp selection?) and whose prompts were tuned
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Start with the purpose (helping a vision-language model choose robot grasps), then the mechanism, and move the PhD-led/ICLR context to a short clause or cut it. Replace the semicolon with a second clause that has its own verb.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed a category-keyed tree index of popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table (Python/SQLAlchemy, Redis cache) to minimize DB queries under access limits
bullet_feedback.problem: 'category-keyed tree index of popular workflows' is a noun stack. '(Python/SQLAlchemy, Redis cache)' is a parenthetical tech dump that doesn't explain any decision. 'under access limits' is unexplained: rate limits, permissions, or quota?
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The constraint that justifies the design (access limits) is the vaguest part of the bullet. A reader can't tell why precomputing was necessary, so the bullet reads as tech plus intent.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'access limits' means (query quota? read-only replica? permission boundary?) and what the index was used for (search? suggestions?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say what the index served and what limit forced it, then mention Redis only if caching was part of the design. Drop the parenthetical; Python and SQLAlchemy can live in Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Shipped a space-research tool used by Amazon Leo’s public-policy team, now maintained by Leo engineers; deployed on AWS Fargate (Docker) via GitHub Actions and CDK (TypeScript)
bullet_feedback.problem: 'space-research tool' doesn't say what the tool does. Everything after the semicolon is a deploy-stack list with two parenthetical tech asides, '(Docker)' and '(TypeScript)'.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the strongest ownership signal on the page: it was shipped, adopted, and handed off. But the reader learns the stack and not the product. 'Shipped' also invites the question of how much of it the candidate built personally, since the role is a team contract.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does for the policy team (e.g. collects/summarizes research?) and the candidate's share of building it
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Spend the words on what the tool does and the handoff. Cut the deploy list down to the one choice worth discussing, or move it to Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member campus product studio that has shipped 5 live products, including Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days; built Redis caching for its Prisma ORM queries
bullet_feedback.problem: Ownership is ambiguous. The 110+ members, 5 products, and 20,000+ visits are org-level results, and the only personal engineering work is a fragment after a semicolon ('built Redis caching for its Prisma ORM queries') with no reason or effect.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical reader will credit the 20,000+ visits to the team, not the candidate. The Redis clause looks like a keyword attached to someone else's success.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the candidate's role on Tortuga and why caching was needed (load from the 20K visits?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Tie the personal contribution to the traffic number in one sentence if it was the reason for the caching. Otherwise separate the founding claim from the engineering claim instead of stitching them together with a semicolon.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut LLM workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by decomposing a Claude skill into sub-skills backed by Python search/validation tools, guided by CloudWatch + OpenSearch latency logs
bullet_feedback.problem: 'LLM workflow generation' and 'Claude skill into sub-skills' are insider terms. A reader doesn't know what is being generated or what a 'skill' is. 'guided by CloudWatch + OpenSearch latency logs' is a tacked-on tech mention with a '+' instead of 'and'.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The metric is clear and has a baseline, but the mechanism is opaque to anyone outside LLM tooling. The trailing clause reads like keyword placement.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what a 'workflow' is here (the same test-data workflows as bullet 1?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Link it explicitly to the workflow builder from the first bullet, and describe the decomposition in plain words (splitting one large prompt into smaller steps that call Python search and validation). Shorten or cut the CloudWatch/OpenSearch clause.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: 'routing ... to inference' drops the noun the reader needs (inference by which model, for what). 'S3 staging hops' is jargon. 6,000+ documents is presented as scale, but it doesn't say whether that is a total or a rate, and 6,000 total is small for a streaming redesign.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer will ask why Kinesis was worth it for 6,000 documents and what the latency was before and after. Without that, the 34% is hard to defend.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 6,000+ is total or per day/run, and what the end-to-end latency was before and after
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say what the pipeline feeds (the classifier from bullet 3?) and state the document volume as a rate if it is one. Keep the S3 to Kinesis swap; it is a real design choice.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing Java policies that tune upper/lower bounds on EC2 capacity reserved for Amazon Redshift operations like patching, balancing availability against cost; initial backtests complete
bullet_feedback.problem: 'Java policies' is vague: it could mean config rules, autoscaling logic, or code. The ending 'initial backtests complete' is a verbless fragment after a semicolon.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top brand on the page, and its only bullet ends in a status note instead of a sentence. 'Policies' leaves unclear whether the candidate designed the tuning logic or implemented rules someone else specified.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the candidate designs the bound-tuning logic or implements given rules
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Make the ending a clause with a verb (e.g. 'and am backtesting them against past usage') and say what a 'policy' decides in plain words.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow builder in React/TypeScript + Electron, adding a React-Flow editor and Jest-tested validation; 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it to the old tool
bullet_feedback.problem: 'legacy test-data workflow builder' is a four-word noun stack, and the reader never learns what the tool does. 'Jest-tested validation' and the '+' joining techs read as compressed, and a semicolon joins the result.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The survey result is credible and well scoped, but a recruiter can't say what the tool is for, so the result has nothing to attach to.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the builder produces (synthetic test data for which systems?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Spend a few words on what the tool lets developers do and trim the tech list to the visual editor, which is the user-facing change.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app (GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search); 93% of generated meals rated satisfactory by internal testers
bullet_feedback.problem: The parenthetical tech dump '(GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search)' and the semicolon-stitched result make this a list, not a sentence. 'RAG meal-suggestion feature' is a noun stack.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The fact that this ships in the official university app is good credibility, but it gets buried. None of the tech names explain a decision.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say what the retrieval is over (dining-hall menus?) in plain words and keep at most one tech name that explains the approach. Join the result with 'and' or a new clause instead of a semicolon.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Shortened research-environment setup time 30% with uv dependency pinning and Docker; added psutil time/memory profiling and Pytest suites to find bottlenecks
bullet_feedback.problem: The semicolon stitches two unrelated tasks, and the second half ends on intent ('to find bottlenecks') with no bottleneck named. 'psutil time/memory profiling' is a compressed noun stack.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is lower-signal than the rest of the page and takes two lines. The profiling half invites 'what did you find?' with no answer on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the profiling found anything concrete
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut the second half or keep only the setup-time claim; consider trimming this bullet if space is needed for clearer wording elsewhere.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Engineered a C++17 order book and matching engine that replayed 50.9M real IEX DEEP+ messages with no resync, matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills exactly and 100% of top-of-book prices
bullet_feedback.problem: 'Engineered' is resume-speak where 'Built' says the same thing. 'with no resync' is jargon a non-trading reader won't parse. It doesn't say what the fills are matched against (IEX's published trades).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The numbers are specific and believable, which is the best kind of evidence. A small wording fix makes it readable to a general SWE screener too.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: matched against what reference (IEX's reported trades?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Use 'Built', and replace 'no resync' with its plain meaning (the book never drifted out of sync with the exchange feed).

bullet_feedback.bullet: Benchmarked B+ tree vs LSM skip-list stores for the simulation’s event logs on identical 2M-record workloads; the B+ tree gave 12.8× read throughput and 22× faster range summaries for 27% more disk
bullet_feedback.problem: 'range summaries' is unexplained, and 'LSM skip-list stores' is a dense noun stack. It is unclear whether the candidate built both stores or benchmarked existing ones.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The trade-off framing ('for 27% more disk') is exactly what interviewers like, but ownership of the two stores is ambiguous, and they would ask.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether both stores were implemented by the candidate
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say 'Built and benchmarked' if true, and use 'range queries' or describe what a range summary computes.

page_feedback.problem: Semicolons stitch clauses in 7 of 14 bullets, and '+' stands in for 'and' in several ('React/TypeScript + Electron', 'CloudWatch + OpenSearch', 'ChromaDB + SentenceBERT').
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the main reason the page reads machine-compressed rather than like a person describing their work. Read aloud, almost every bullet needs re-punctuating.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Allow at most one semicolon on the page. Rewrite stitched bullets as one sentence with a connecting verb, or cut the weaker half.

page_feedback.problem: Several bullets never say what the system does for its users ('space-research tool', 'test-data workflow builder', 'document-importance classifier', 'Java policies') and spend the words on stack names instead.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This fails the plain-language test. A recruiter can repeat the brands and techs but not the products, which weakens the 'shipped real systems' story the page is meant to tell.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Give each system a short purpose clause before the tech, and move tech that doesn't explain a decision to Skills.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists items that appear nowhere in the experience (X-Ray, SNS, API Gateway, PyTorch, Node.js) next to ones that are demonstrated.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical interviewer may probe the undemonstrated ones. Keyword-only entries thin out the credibility of the list.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only items the candidate can discuss in depth, or accept the risk knowingly.

page_feedback.problem: The most technically distinctive and verifiable work (the IEX matching engine, with its exact fill match and throughput) sits at the bottom, after five roles of mostly cloud-glue bullets.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: On a 7-second skim, the 'performance-sensitive systems' half of the intended profile is easy to miss.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the section order (experience first is standard for interns), but make sure the earlier bullets are plain enough that the reader reaches Projects.

keep: Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, averaging 686.7 ns/event in the matching engine
The 'matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills exactly' figure in the IEX bullet
The '90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it to the old tool' result
The 'for 27% more disk' trade-off framing in the B+ tree benchmark bullet
Clean one-page layout with right-aligned dates and sparse bold metrics
